stem: A client using continuous glucose monitoring says, “My insurance changed and I may not be able to afford the sensors next month.” Which nursing action best supports equitable diabetes care?

options.A: Assess the financial and insurance barrier, notify the diabetes care team, and connect the client with appropriate coverage, social-service, or lower-cost support resources before access is interrupted.
options.B: Assume technology access depends only on personal preference and continue the plan without addressing cost or coverage.
options.C: Tell the client to stop using diabetes technology permanently because financial barriers cannot be modified by the care team.
options.D: Wait until the client has already run out of sensors before discussing access because insurance status is not relevant to treatment planning.

rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care direct clinicians to assess financial barriers, health insurance, and health care access as social determinants that can affect diabetes management and to collaborate with the care team and social-service resources to reduce cost-related barriers. ADA also recognizes geographic and socioeconomic variation in diabetes-technology adoption and emphasizes continued access to devices and supplies. B, C, and D fail to address a modifiable barrier that can disrupt evidence-based care.
educational_objective: Identify and address financial or insurance barriers to diabetes technology early by coordinating coverage and support resources to reduce avoidable interruption of effective therapy.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
source_document_title: Improving Care and Promoting Health in Populations: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; Diabetes Technology: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_locator: Section 1 Recommendations 1.6–1.7 — assess insurance status, financial barriers, health insurance and health care access and refer to resources; Section 9 Recommendation 9.29 — routinely assess financial obstacles and collaborate to reduce costs; Section 7 — geographic and socioeconomic variation in pump/AID adoption and need for continued technology access
source_claim_supported: Financial, insurance, socioeconomic, and access barriers can affect diabetes care and technology use; current ADA guidance requires assessment of such barriers and collaborative efforts to preserve access to evidence-based treatment and supplies.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care; identify barriers to care, coordinate referrals/resources, support continuity, and advocate for access to prescribed treatment
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — financial barriers and equitable access to diabetes technology
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source abstract disparities item into a nursing care-coordination scenario. The final item tests the actionable ADA 2026 requirement to assess and address insurance/financial barriers rather than simply asking the learner to recall that disparities exist.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: health equity / diabetes technology access / financial barriers
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sections 1, 7, and 9. The source directly identifies insurance/financial barriers and socioeconomic/geographic variation in technology access and recommends collaborative barrier reduction.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A translates the current standards into a nursing coordination action without promising a particular insurance outcome or assistance program. No specific payer rule is invented.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it assesses the barrier and mobilizes appropriate resources before therapy interruption.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; technology access is influenced by systemic and financial factors, not preference alone.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; the standards call for collaborative barrier-reduction efforts rather than automatic discontinuation.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; insurance and financial access are relevant to treatment planning and should be assessed proactively.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A addresses both the identified barrier and continuity of prescribed care.
audit_findings.cueing: All options concern the care team’s response to an access problem.
audit_findings.blueprint: Management of Care is directly appropriate because the nurse is coordinating resources and continuity while addressing a social determinant of health.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked insurance/financial claims, technology-access evidence, guarantee-versus-support wording, social-services scope, geographic/socioeconomic nuance, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
